narrative:
The promotion was denied because the model estimated a 41% probability that you will leave—roughly four in ten employees with a similar profile are expected to depart. That is not a certainty, but it was treated as a material retention risk in the promotion decision. Gender, age, and health issues were not used.

The most influential factor was your overall work experience. At 1–5 years, you are in the same range as about half of employees predicted to stay, and this factor pushed your estimated risk downward rather than upward. The second most influential factor was whether you had other job opportunities. You reported none; because most employees predicted to stay also reported none, this also lowered your leave risk. The third most influential factor was how easy it was to get involved in the job—decision-making and having your opinions heard. You found this difficult, while only about one in ten employees predicted to stay said the same. That difficulty raised your predicted risk of leaving.

Other signals in your profile—such as no annual bonus, dissatisfaction with rewards for effort, not feeling you received the deserved promotion, low emotional commitment, no recognition, and no training in the last three years—added to the concern. Before promotion is reconsidered, you and your manager should address involvement and voice, recognition and rewards, training, and clear promotion criteria. The organization should verify whether the 41% risk is actionable rather than treating it as automatic exclusion.
